title: Microbiology Paper 4: Viruses, Immunity and Microbial Classification
source: Adapted from user-provided Dentistry past paper questions (Microbiology pages)

objective.question: Substances that are used against microorganisms may be described as:
objective.explanation: Anti-microbial agents are described by their action as cidal (killing) or static (inhibiting), e.g. bactericidal, bacteriostatic, fungicidal.

objective.question: Which of the following diseases is NOT caused by a virus?
objective.explanation: Bubonic plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis; smallpox, influenza, AIDS and SARS are viral diseases.

objective.question: Which of the following signs and symptoms is not linked to Haemophilus influenzae?
objective.explanation: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted by mosquitoes; H. influenzae causes otitis media, pneumonia, epiglottitis and meningitis.

objective.question: Which of the following is not a DNA virus?
objective.explanation: Caliciviruses carry a single-stranded RNA genome; adenoviruses, papovaviruses (papillomaviruses/polyomaviruses) and poxviruses are DNA viruses.

objective.question: Which of the following is not an RNA virus?
objective.explanation: Herpesviruses have double-stranded DNA genomes; reoviruses, orthomyxoviruses (influenza) and hepatitis delta virus are RNA viruses.

objective.question: Edward Jenner's main contribution to the science of immunology was that he:
options: Invented the disposable syringe and needle
objective.explanation: In 1796 Edward Jenner introduced vaccination with cowpox to protect against smallpox, founding the practice of immunisation.

objective.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of antibodies?
options: Stimulate formation of the membrane attack complex by complement
Neutralise pathogens by binding to them
Display antigens on the surface of antigen-presenting cells
objective.explanation: Antigen display on MHC molecules is a function of antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells, not of antibodies.

objective.question: Which of the following statements about helper T cells is FALSE?
options: Helper T cells stimulate B cells to proliferate
Helper T cells assist cytotoxic T lymphocytes in killing infected cells
Helper T cells stimulate antibody production by B cells
Helper T cells present antigens with MHC class II molecules to other lymphocytes
objective.explanation: Helper T cells recognise antigen presented on MHC class II by antigen-presenting cells; they do not themselves present antigen with MHC class II to other lymphocytes.

objective.question: Which of the following is NOT a property of the innate immune system?
options: Uses physical barriers such as skin and certain cells of the body
Is the body's primary line of defence
objective.explanation: Specificity and immunological memory are properties of adaptive immunity; the innate system acts rapidly and non-specifically.

objective.question: Which of the following is NOT true of the adaptive immune system?
options: It has memory of prior infections
It can adapt to specific threats
It produces antibodies to fight disease
It responds immediately to germ exposure
objective.explanation: Adaptive responses take days to develop on first exposure because lymphocytes must be activated and expanded; the innate response is the immediate one.

objective.question: Monocytes move from the systemic circulatory system into general connective tissues, where they differentiate into which phagocytic cell type?
objective.explanation: Blood monocytes leave the circulation and mature into tissue macrophages (or dendritic cells) that phagocytose debris and pathogens.

objective.question: Which of the following microorganisms is NOT matched correctly with its isolation medium?
objective.explanation: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is isolated on selective media such as Thayer-Martin (which produces green colonies on GC agar), not on pink-colony (MacConkey) media, which select Gram-negative enterics.

objective.question: Normal flora would typically have what type of relationship with its host?
objective.explanation: Normal flora are classically commensals: they benefit from the host without harming it, although many interactions are also mutually beneficial.

objective.question: What is a nosocomial infection?
options: An infection of the mucous membrane of the nose
An infection acquired from a health care environment
An infection transmitted by nasal secretions
An infection acquired while travelling abroad
objective.explanation: Nosocomial (healthcare-associated) infections are acquired in hospitals or other healthcare facilities rather than in the community.

objective.question: Which of the following best describes what a pandemic is?
options: An infectious disease that kills people quickly
A vaccination programme that eliminates an infectious disease
An infectious disease that kills a large number of people
An infectious disease that spreads across a large geographic region
objective.explanation: A pandemic is an epidemic that spreads over several countries or continents, affecting a large proportion of the population.

objective.question: Disinfectants are substances that are:
options: Most effective at high protein content
Not generally used to eradicate microorganisms from inanimate material
objective.explanation: Disinfectants reduce microbial numbers on inanimate objects but, with the exception of strong sporicidal agents, do not reliably kill bacterial spores.

objective.question: What is a key difference between the lytic and the lysogenic viral life cycles?
options: Cells are lysed in the lysogenic cycle; they are not lysed in the lytic cycle
Viral DNA or RNA is incorporated into the host genome in the lytic cycle and not in the lysogenic cycle
New virions are assembled and released immediately during the lysogenic cycle
Cells are lysed in the lytic cycle; they are not lysed in the lysogenic cycle
When the lysogenic cycle is initiated, the virus can never later enter the lytic cycle
objective.explanation: In the lytic cycle the host cell is lysed as new virions are released, whereas in the lysogenic cycle the viral genome persists in the host without immediate lysis (and may later be induced into the lytic cycle).

objective.question: Which term refers to a viral life cycle that leads to the immediate production of progeny, destruction of the host cell, and release of many virions?
objective.explanation: The lytic cycle ends with burst of the host cell and release of newly assembled virions.

objective.question: A DNA virus that infects humans and incorporates its genetic material into the host's genome is best described as:
objective.explanation: Integration of a DNA viral genome into the host chromosome with continued presence of the virus is the lysogenic (temperate) pattern, as seen with herpesviruses and HPV.

objective.question: The major role of T cells in the immune response includes which one of the following?
options: Recognition of epitopes presented with major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules on cell surfaces
objective.explanation: T cells recognise antigen fragments presented on MHC molecules; antibody production is by plasma (B-lineage) cells and phagocytosis by innate cells.

structured.question: Define zoonotic diseases. (4 marks)
markingGuide: Definition: diseases transmissible between animals and humans
Mention that the causative agents spread from animals directly or via products/secretions
Credit any correct example, e.g. rabies, brucellosis, anthrax
Credit a note on the animal reservoir or vector
structured.modelAnswer: Zoonotic diseases are infections that are naturally transmissible from vertebrate animals to humans; they may be spread by direct contact with infected animals, by ingestion of contaminated animal products, by arthropod vectors or by aerosols (examples include rabies, anthrax, brucellosis and salmonellosis).

structured.question: Name at least three (3) bacteria that cause zoonotic diseases in humans. (4 marks)
markingGuide: Any three of: Bacillus anthracis, Brucella species, Leptospira species
Also acceptable: Yersinia pestis, Coxiella burnetii, Mycobacterium bovis, Francisella tularensis
One mark per correct organism, up to three
One mark for correct spelling/presentation
structured.modelAnswer: Three examples are Bacillus anthracis (anthrax), Brucella species (brucellosis) and Leptospira species (leptospirosis); other correct answers include Mycobacterium bovis, Yersinia pestis, Coxiella burnetii and Francisella tularensis.

structured.question: Bacteria are classified into Gram-negative and Gram-positive. Using a table, describe the stepwise procedure of Gram staining. (12 marks)
markingGuide: Table format with reagent / step / time / result columns
Step 1: flood smear with crystal violet (primary stain) for about 1 minute - all cells appear purple
Step 2: add Gram's iodine (mordant) for about 1 minute - forms crystal violet-iodine complex
Step 3: decolourise with alcohol or acetone for a few seconds - Gram-positive retain purple, Gram-negative lose colour
Step 4: counterstain with safranin for about 1 minute - Gram-negative appear red/pink, Gram-positive remain purple
Step 5: blot dry, examine under oil immersion; credit control organisms and interpretation
structured.modelAnswer: Gram staining proceeds: (1) crystal violet for 1 minute, rinsing with water between steps; (2) Gram's iodine as mordant for 1 minute; (3) rapid decolourisation with 95% alcohol or acetone until runoff is clear; (4) safranin counterstain for 1 minute; (5) blot dry and view under the oil-immersion lens. Gram-positive bacteria retain the purple crystal violet-iodine complex because of their thick peptidoglycan, while Gram-negative bacteria take up the red safranin and appear pink.

structured.question:
Cells can be divided into prokaryotes and eukaryotes. (12 marks)
(a) Define prokaryotes and give two examples. (6 marks)
(b) Define eukaryotes and give two examples. (6 marks)
markingGuide: (a) Definition: simple cells lacking a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles
(a) Two examples: bacteria (e.g. Escherichia coli) and archaea
(a) Note absence of histones/80S-type organisation, circular chromosome in nucleoid
(b) Definition: cells with a true membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
(b) Two examples: animal cells (e.g. human epithelial cell) and plant cells (e.g. onion cell)
(b) Note linear chromosomes, mitosis, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum
structured.modelAnswer: (a) Prokaryotes are simple cells in which the genetic material lies free in the cytoplasm (nucleoid) without a surrounding nuclear membrane and which lack membrane-bound organelles; examples are bacteria such as Escherichia coli and archaea. (b) Eukaryotes are cells that contain a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane together with membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum; examples are human (animal) cells and plant cells.

structured.question: List four (4) common characteristics of microorganisms. (8 marks)
markingGuide: They are microscopic, i.e. too small to be seen with the naked eye
They are composed largely of water and organic molecules with a cellular structure
They reproduce mainly by binary fission, budding or spore formation
They require nutrients, moisture, suitable pH and temperature for growth
Credit any other valid shared characteristic, e.g. ability to cause disease or exist as saprophytes
structured.modelAnswer: Common characteristics of microorganisms include: they are microscopic in size; they have a cellular organisation (prokaryotic or eukaryotic) containing water, proteins, carbohydrates and nucleic acids; they reproduce rapidly by fission, budding or sporulation; and they require nutrients, moisture, suitable temperature and pH to grow, with many able to cause disease or to live as saprophytes.
